clinicalPearls: A markedly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with NO bleeding tendency is the hallmark and most important teaching point.
It is usually discovered incidentally during preoperative screening or the workup of an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time.
Factor XII drives the contact activation (intrinsic) pathway in vitro but is dispensable for physiological haemostasis in vivo, which is initiated by tissue factor.
A mixing study corrects the prolonged clotting time, confirming factor deficiency rather than an inhibitor; prothrombin time and thrombin time are normal.
Essential surgery and anticoagulation should not be withheld or delayed on the basis of the laboratory abnormality alone.
Historically linked to thrombosis — the index patient, John Hageman, died of pulmonary embolism — but a causal thrombotic role is not established.
Other contact factor deficiencies (prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen) similarly prolong the activated partial thromboplastin time without bleeding.
Gain-of-function F12 mutations cause a form of hereditary angioedema, a distinct disorder that must not be confused with factor deficiency.
reference.pathophysiology: Factor XII (Hageman factor), encoded by F12 and synthesised in the liver, is a zymogen activated on contact with negatively charged surfaces, together with prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen forming the contact activation system. Activated factor XIIa converts factor XI to XIa, propagating the intrinsic cascade measured by the activated partial thromboplastin time, and also cleaves prekallikrein to kallikrein, driving the kallikrein-kinin system that generates bradykinin. Although essential for surface-initiated clotting in the test tube, factor XII is not required for haemostasis in vivo, where coagulation is triggered by the tissue factor and factor VIIa pathway; consequently its congenital deficiency, usually autosomal recessive from F12 mutations, greatly prolongs the activated partial thromboplastin time yet causes no clinical bleeding. Because factor XIIa also contributes to thrombus propagation and to inflammatory and complement pathways, its deficiency has been proposed to modulate thrombotic risk, but this association remains controversial and unproven.
additionalDifferentials: Lupus anticoagulant or antiphospholipid antibodies (prolonged clotting time with thrombotic rather than bleeding risk)
Haemophilia A or B (prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time WITH bleeding — the key contrast)
von Willebrand disease with a secondarily reduced factor VIII
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time with immediate and incubated mixing studies
Prothrombin time and thrombin time (expected normal)
Assays for prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen if factor XII is normal
Lupus anticoagulant testing including dilute Russell viper venom time
Specific assays for factors VIII, IX and XI to exclude a true bleeding disorder
F12 genetic analysis where clinically relevant
redFlags: The prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time being misattributed and prompting unnecessary plasma or blood product transfusion
Genuine bleeding symptoms, which should trigger a search for an alternative or coexisting disorder
New arterial or venous thrombosis, warranting a standard thrombophilia assessment
Delay or cancellation of essential surgery driven solely by the laboratory result
reference.prognosis: Excellent; isolated factor XII deficiency does not cause a bleeding disorder, generally requires no treatment, and is compatible with normal life expectancy.
pitfalls: Transfusing plasma or delaying surgery because of the prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time — the central error to avoid.
Assuming that any prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time signifies a bleeding risk.
Missing a coexisting true bleeding disorder when bleeding is genuinely present.
Confusing factor XII deficiency with factor XII-related hereditary angioedema caused by gain-of-function mutations.
Omitting a mixing study, which is needed to distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor or lupus anticoagulant.
management: Reassurance and no haemostatic treatment, as isolated factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding
Confirmation of the diagnosis with a correcting mixing study and factor XII assay, and exclusion of a lupus anticoagulant or a true intrinsic-pathway factor deficiency before procedures
Proceeding with necessary surgery and anticoagulation without delay despite the prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time
Clear documentation and flagging of the abnormality to prevent unnecessary plasma transfusion and repeated investigation
Standard thromboprophylaxis and anticoagulation given as clinically indicated for any coexisting condition
No specific surveillance required, with reassurance regarding the recessive inheritance
